PART A
Question #1

a. Create a vector
```{r}
scores <- c(Ana = 78, Ben = 92, Cid = 85, Dex = 92, Eli = 67, Fay = 88, Gio = 74)
scores
```
b. Sort the scores in ascending order and descending order. What is the output?
```{r}
sorted_asc <- sort(scores)
sorted_desc <- sort(scores, decreasing = TRUE)

sorted_asc
sorted_desc
```
c. Print your sorted result from sort-ascending. Check whether the # names (“Ana”, “Ben”, …) stayed attached to their correct values.
```{r}
print(sorted_asc)
```

-Yes, the names stayed to their values.

d. Create another vectors:
```{r}
subjects <- c("Science", "Math", "English", "Filipino", "PE")
incomplete <- c(85, NA, 90, 70, NA, 95)
```
e. Sort subjects alphabetically using sort()
```{r}
sort(subjects)
```
f. Sort incomplete using sort(). Observe what happens to the NA
```{r}
sort(incomplete)
```
sort removed the NA

Question #2

- Yes, the names stayed attached to their correct values. This matters because there is a possibility that you might credit someone with 99 who actually scored 50 if the names did not stay to their correct values.

Question #3

- There is so many possibilities a student might get an NA score. It's either they cheated or did not get the exam and using sort() silently removes that NA and the lowest recorded score might not be the actual lowest.

Question #4
```{r}
order(scores)
sort(scores)
```
- sort() returns the values with names and order() prints the positions 
a. Use the result of order(scores) to index scores itself: # Compare this to sort(scores) – they should produce the same values.
```{r}
scores[order(scores)]
```
- Yes, they have the same values. putting order() inside scores[] returns the elements in that order

Question #5
```{r}
students <- data.frame(
  name    = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli", "Fay", "Gio"),
  score   = c(78, 92, 85, 92, 67, 88, 74),
  section = c("A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "B", "A")
)
students
```
a. Reorder the ENTIRE students data frame by score using students[order(students$score), ]
```{r}
students[order(students$score), ]
```

b. Reorder students by score in DESCENDING order.
```{r}
students[order(students$score, decreasing = TRUE), ]
```

Question #6

- order() only returns the positions of the elements. It's useless on its own because there is no actual data.

Question #7

- sort() only works on a single vector, and it returns the values themselves in sorted order. order() is the right tool because it returns row positions rather than values, so using it in students[order(students$score), ] moves every column together and keeps the related columns lined up.

Question #8
```{r}
scores <- c(Ana = 78, Ben = 92, Cid = 85, Dex = 92, Eli = 67, Fay = 88, Gio = 74)
scores

rank(scores)
cbind(scores, rank = rank(scores))
```
a. Ranking output for Ben and Dex
```{r}
rank(scores)[c("Ben", "Dex")]
```
b. Ben and Dex both scored 92, the highest score in the class, but under the default rank() they did NOT both simply get rank “1” or rank “7” as a whole number. Explain exactly what value they received by default and why R computes it that way for tied values.

- By default, rank() gives tied values the average of the ranks they would have occupied, so Ben and Dex, who tie for ranks 6 and 7, each receive (6 + 7) / 2 = 6.5.

Question #8
a. Create the data frame and add the rank column

- Add a column sales$rank that ranks employees by units_sold, with the TOP seller receiving rank 1.
```{r}
sales <- data.frame(
  employee = c("Rey", "Sam", "Tin", "Uma", "Val"),
  units_sold = c(120, 145, 145, 98, 130)
)

sales$rank <- rank(-sales$units_sold)
sales
```

b. Reorder the entire sales data frame using order() so it is displayed from HIGHEST units_sold to LOWEST.
```{r}
sales[order(sales$units_sold, decreasing = TRUE), ]
```

Questions #9

- order() only tells you where each row should be placed, so it cannot award standings by itself. rank() gives each value its standing and handles ties, which is why Sam and Tin, who both sold 145, share rank 1.5.
